transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-12-11 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Ethan Park, Sofia Alvarez (Redwood); Priya Sinha, Carlos Ruiz, Leah Morgan, Tom Becker (Helios)

Summary (auto): Hybrid SLO mix: TTFT for interactive assistant, TPOT for batch planning jobs; p95/p99 targets debated; measurement & sampling plan agreed.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining from both sides. quick roll call?
[00:06] Priya Sinha: priya here, hi.
[00:09] Carlos Ruiz: carlos — platform, hello.
[00:12] Leah Morgan: leah, s r e, hi.
[00:15] Tom Becker: tom, ml lead.
[00:18] Maya Chen: perfect. so agenda — define success criteria for the pilot, pick TTFT vs TPOT anchors per flow, agree sampling/benchmark plan and timeline. Ethan do you want to kickoff with the measurement framing?
[00:29] Ethan Park: yep, sure. so quick framing: we've seen customers split flows into interactive (user-facing chat/assistant) where TTFT matters strongly, and background or batch inference where TPOT (total per-request tokens) is the cost/throughput metric. for helio, you mentioned two primary workloads earlier?
[00:48] Tom Becker: yeah — one is the operator assistant, very interactive, median prompt length ~120 tokens, responses ~80 tokens; the other is our mission planning batch job — long sequences, often 1–2k tokens per request but run asynchronously.
[01:05] Ethan Park: okay that maps nicely to TTFT for the assistant and TPOT for planning. question is SLO targets — what's realistic? helio, do you have internal p95/p99 goals today?
[01:16] Carlos Ruiz: right now it's messy — our app-level p95 for assistant RPC is ~300ms in region most of the time but spikes. we wanted to see if we could get to under 150 ms p95 for first token ideally.
[01:29] Leah Morgan: p99 is our pain point — when crews hit spikes it goes to 1.5–2 seconds which impacts operator flow.
[01:36] Maya Chen: okay so proposed starting SLOs: TTFT p95 <= 150ms, TTFT p99 <= 400ms for the interactive flow. for batch/TPOT we propose p95 end-to-end throughput target tied to 90% of baseline cost per 1k tokens — essentially average TPOT under Xms per 1k tokens. it's okay if we calibrate after the first run.
[01:55] Priya Sinha: that p99 400ms feels optimistic but it's a good objective. question — does the TTFT number include network egress, LB latency and our app code or is that strictly Redwood runtime?
[02:09] Sofia Alvarez: good question — our standard SLO framing is three tiers: app-to-redwood TTFT (what the customer observes), runtime-only TTFT (our service time), and blended. for the pilot we'll measure both: raw runtime TTFT and end-to-end from your edge to first token. when we report SLOs we'll show both so you can map to your app-level objectives.
[02:31] Tom Becker: can you also decompose the time — like kernel time vs queuing vs K V cache hit time? we have a lot of cache locality in planning jobs.
[02:40] Ethan Park: yes we'll include a breakdown. small note — sometimes the transcript engine mislabels K V cache as K V cash in our logs, ha, so we'll annotate.
[02:49] Carlos Ruiz: (laughs) noted.
[02:52] Maya Chen: moving on — sampling and benchmark plan. we usually ask for a 7-day production sample to capture diurnal and weekday spikes. helio mentioned you could only share 72 hours in a first tranche?
[03:04] Carlos Ruiz: we can do 72 to start, redacted. we can flag spike windows and a few full traces for deep analysis.
[03:11] Ethan Park: that works. Plan: Redwood will run a 48-hour synthetic benchmark that replays your traces with three modalities: 1) replay as-is (preserves inter-arrival), 2) compressed replay where we increase burstiness to simulate high concurrent load, 3) steady ramp test. We'll capture TTFT runtime-only and end-to-end TPOT metrics, token counts, queue depths, kernel selection, and quantization profile effects.
[03:38] Leah Morgan: what's the sample size for stat confidence on p99? we want to avoid false negatives from low sample counts.
[03:44] Ethan Park: good call. for p99 we need at least ~10k requests in the measurement window to get decent stability. if your interactive flow is lower volume, we'll stitch in synthetic traffic to reach minimum sample size. we'll annotate which points are synthetic.
[03:58] Priya Sinha: how do we treat cold KV cache runs? our planning job often hits cold weights in big sequences.
[04:05] Sofia Alvarez: we'll separate cold-start samples — mark them explicitly. for acceptance we'll look at warm-state p95/p99 primarily but we'll also quantify cold-start tail and propose mitigations (prefetch, pinned cache, warm-up replicas).
[04:19] Tom Becker: on model variants: we plan to test two variants — a 16-bit quantized medium model and a 4-bit quantized variant that has slightly lower quality but much lower latency/cost. can we get a quality delta measurement?
[04:30] Ethan Park: yes, we'll run automatic evals on your prompt set and report rouge/semantic similarity metrics and example failure modes. we'll also run a small human-in-the-loop review for edge cases you flag.
[04:43] Maya Chen: let's talk SLO composition — hybrid approach. recommendation is to have hard TTFT SLOs for interactive, a cost/throughput SLA for batch, and a fallback routing policy that moves requests to a smaller model variant during sustained overloads. thoughts?
[04:58] Carlos Ruiz: that sounds right. what about canarying and rollbacks? we need a safe ramp plan.
[05:04] Sofia Alvarez: Redwood supports canaries by percent or by token cost threshold. for pilot we'll propose a canary config: 5% traffic -> 25% -> 60% over a day with automatic rollback if p95 degrades >20% or error rate increases.
[05:18] Leah Morgan: for compliance, during pilot some traces will contain PII; we need to ensure redaction and that everything sent to Redwood's hosted nodes is encrypted at rest.
[05:27] Maya Chen: yes — we support envelope encryption and we can run Dedicated private burst nodes within your VPC for any PII flows. we'll share SOC2 and data handling docs.
[05:36] Tom Becker: curious on how cache prefetch helps TTFT on the interactive path. we see many similar prompts in operator flows.
[05:42] Ethan Park: prefix/KV caching is effective — for repeated prompts it'll shave off the KV lookup and early attention compute. in practice we've seen 20–40% TTFT reductions for high-locality workloads. we'll run a cache-ablation test as part of the benchmark.
[05:57] Priya Sinha: okay timeline? when can Redwood run the 48-hour benchmark?
[06:01] Maya Chen: we can start as soon as we have the 72-hour trace subset and signed NDA addendum for traces — propose start 2028-12-13, finish 2028-12-15, then follow up deep-dive on 2028-12-19. does that align?
[06:12] Carlos Ruiz: yes that works.
[06:15] Leah Morgan: for the 48-hour run, will Redwood host the runner or do we run it in our env?
[06:20] Ethan Park: Redwood will host the benchmark runner but we can provide a containerized runner you can execute in your environment for verification. both results will be shared.
[06:29] Tom Becker: on reporting — please include distribution histograms, not only p95/p99 numbers; we want to see mode, mean, stdev.
[06:36] Maya Chen: absolutely. plus tokenized latency curves, queue depth over time, and kernel selection heatmaps.
[06:42] Priya Sinha: what about traffic shaping? we sometimes throttle clients upstream; how will that affect SLO measurement?
[06:48] Sofia Alvarez: we'll run a traffic shaping matrix to emulate your throttles — baseline, no-throttle, partial throttle. all will be in the benchmark. we'll annotate the traces used.
[07:00] Carlos Ruiz: risk question — what if in production a sudden edgeburst causes sustained degradation; do you have automatic fallback to older model or to simpler heuristic?
[07:08] Ethan Park: yes — fallback policy can do model variant downgrade, route to dedicated reserved capacity if available, or degrade gracefully to a cached answer with a limited response size. for critical paths you can configure immediate fallback thresholds.
[07:20] Leah Morgan: can we surface the exact cause when an SLO breach happens? we need triage signals.
[07:25] Maya Chen: Redwood Console will show per-request traces with timing breakdowns; we'll include alerting hooks to your pager and synthetic checks.
[07:33] Tom Becker: let's record the proposed acceptance criteria quickly: 1) Interactive TTFT p95 <= 150ms, p99 <= 400ms; actual end-to-end app-level p95 <= 250ms (taking your LB and app overhead into account); 2) Batch TPOT — cost per 1k tokens within 10% of baseline or better; 3) Quality delta for quantized variant <= defined threshold on your eval set.
[07:56] Maya Chen: I'll capture that in the pilot charter. anyone strongly disagree?
[08:00] Priya Sinha: fine, but want higher p99 guardrails in canary if possible.
[08:04] Sofia Alvarez: we'll tighten rollback thresholds on p99 for canary.
[08:08] Carlos Ruiz: ok.
[08:10] Ethan Park: a couple of measurement nuances: 1) p99 needs time-alignment — we'll use sliding windows and ensure bootstrap confidence intervals; 2) for TPOT we prefer measuring per-1k tokens to normalize across variable-length responses.
[08:25] Leah Morgan: what about sample alignment for p99 when you stitch synthetic traffic? how do you avoid bias?
[08:30] Ethan Park: we'll tag synthetic and real samples and provide separate p99s and a combined p99 with weighting that reflects your production proportions. transparency is key.
[08:40] Tom Becker: any thoughts on minimum run length for TPOT stability?
[08:43] Ethan Park: for TPOT, because token distributions have long tails, we recommend at least 24–48 hours with a few thousand long sequences to get stable estimates. that's why the 48-hour benchmark + 7-day trace export works well.
[08:57] Maya Chen: ok we're at 40 minutes in — quick round of questions from helio?
[09:02] Priya Sinha: when you talk about dedicated burst nodes in our VPC, is the orchestration still managed by Redwood?
[09:08] Sofia Alvarez: yes orchestration remains Redwood-managed but the nodes live in your VPC and network controls are yours. access is via mutual TLS and optional HSM-managed keys.
[09:18] Carlos Ruiz: will logs for the pilot be stored in our logging account or Redwood's?
[09:22] Maya Chen: both options — we can push structured logs to your ingestion endpoint and keep a mirror in Redwood for observability.
[09:30] Leah Morgan: about encryption, we want end-to-end encryption for PII — can you support customer-managed KMS in the Dedicated config?
[09:36] Sofia Alvarez: yes, customer-managed KMS is supported for keys at rest in dedicated & private deployment options. we'll include the config template.
[09:45] Tom Becker: small nit — can the benchmark measure model warmup jitter when autoscaling happens during a burst? that's often where p99 suffers.
[09:53] Ethan Park: yes we'll include autoscale stress tests and capture warmup latency per replica. We'll also test pre-warm policies.
[09:59] Maya Chen: i'm going to read back the commitments and next steps — to make sure we're aligned. Redwood: deliver benchmark script and run 48-hour burstiness benchmark starting 2028-12-13; share raw CSV, histograms, kernel heatmaps; provide canary config and pilot charter. Helios: provide 72-hour trace subset asap and 7-day redacted traces; share security contact for SOC2 review.
[10:22] Priya Sinha: yes, we will send traces by 2028-12-14 and SOC2 contact by 2028-12-13.
[10:27] Maya Chen: will also send pricing sketch and pilot charter by 2028-12-15.
[10:32] Carlos Ruiz: one more ask — include a short appendix on how to interpret TTFT vs TPOT tradeoffs so our execs can sign off.
[10:38] Maya Chen: noted, will include a 1-page executive appendix.
[10:41] Leah Morgan: ok great. thanks everyone.
[10:43] Maya Chen: thanks all — we’ll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark kickoff and the deep dive on 2028-12-19.

Auto action summary (end):
- Redwood to run 48hr benchmark, produce detailed metrics and artifacts.
- Helios to provide traces and security contacts.
- Follow-up deep-dive scheduled.
